questions.prompt: Which of these request methods is NOT defined as idempotent by RFC 9110?

options.text: PUT
DELETE
POST
GET

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines PUT, DELETE and the safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) as idempotent. POST is not in that list, so repeating a POST is not guaranteed to have the same intended effect as sending it once; for example, it might create a second resource.

questions.prompt: DELETE is defined as a safe method by RFC 9110.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines only GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe among its methods. DELETE is idempotent, but it is not safe because it requests a state change on the server.

questions.prompt: According to RFC 9110, what makes a request method idempotent?

options.text: Every identical request receives an identical response, including the same status code
The intended effect on the server of several identical requests is the same as the effect of a single request
The client does not request or expect any state change on the origin server
The server records no side effects, such as log entries, for repeated requests

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines idempotency by the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests, not by the response, which might differ when a request is repeated. A server is still free to log each request separately or keep other per-request side effects, and "no requested state change" is the definition of a safe method, not an idempotent one.

questions.prompt: A request is sent, and the connection closes before any response is received. Which statement about automatic retries matches RFC 9110?

options.text: A retried PUT is guaranteed to receive the same response as the original request
A proxy may automatically retry a POST in this situation, because no response was received
A client must never retry automatically, because the original request might already have been applied
The client can retry a PUT on a new connection, because repeating it has the same intended effect even if the original succeeded

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 uses this PUT case as its example: the client can open a new connection and retry the idempotent request, although the response might differ. In contrast, a proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests such as POST, and a client SHOULD NOT automatically retry them unless it knows the request is actually idempotent or was never applied.

questions.prompt: According to RFC 9110, what is the fundamental difference between PUT and POST?

options.text: PUT asks that the enclosed representation replace the target resource's state; POST asks the target resource to process it according to its own semantics
PUT can only modify existing resources, while only POST can create new ones
PUT responses are cacheable, while POST responses are never cacheable
PUT is a safe method, while POST is not

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 says the representation enclosed in a PUT is defined as replacing the state of the target resource, whereas the target of a POST handles it according to the resource's own semantics. This is why the intent of PUT is idempotent, and a PUT can also create the target resource when it has no current representation.

questions.prompt: RFC 5789 defines the PATCH method as idempotent, just like PUT.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: RFC 5789 states that PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent. Unlike a PUT, which carries a modified version of the resource to replace the stored one, a PATCH carries a set of instructions describing how to modify the current resource. A PATCH request can still be issued in an idempotent way, and RFC 5789 says clients whose patch format needs a known base point SHOULD use a conditional request, for example `If-Match` with a strong ETag.

questions.prompt: How does a HEAD request differ from a GET request for the same resource?

options.text: HEAD responses are never cacheable, while GET responses are
The server must omit every header field it would send in response to GET
The server must not send content in the response, but otherwise HEAD is identical to GET
HEAD is not a safe method, because it can change the resource's metadata

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines HEAD as identical to GET except that the server MUST NOT send content in the response, so it is used to obtain metadata without transferring the representation data. The server SHOULD send the same header fields it would send for GET, HEAD is a safe method, and responses to HEAD are cacheable.

questions.prompt: Besides GET and HEAD, which method does RFC 9110 define caching semantics for, with responses cacheable only when they include explicit freshness information and a `Content-Location` equal to the request's target URI?

options.text: PUT
POST
DELETE
OPTIONS

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines caching semantics for GET, HEAD and POST, and a POST response is cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a `Content-Location` that has the same value as the POST's target URI. Even then, a cached POST response can satisfy only a later GET or HEAD, never another POST, and RFC 9110 defines responses to PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS as not cacheable.
